name: Alar base reduction (alarplasty)

lead: Alar base reduction removes small wedges of tissue near the nostril wing to make wide or flared nostrils narrower. The payoff is a slimmer-looking nose base, visible once healed.

It is most often combined with rhinoplasty, and on looksmaxxing forums it appears mostly in before-and-after photo threads where posters debate how much change a given face needs. Published research is mainly technique descriptions and classification studies, including work on how the alar region moves during a smile, rather than trials of cosmetic satisfaction.

paras: Small wedges of skin and soft tissue are removed from the nostril sill or the alar-facial junction and the wound is closed, reducing nostril width. It is done on its own or together with a nose job.

As a change to the nostril opening, it has been studied for effects on breathing, and some functional nasal surgery reports link nostril reduction to airflow concerns. Scarring and asymmetry are general surgical concerns. It is performed by surgeons.

angle.text: Alarplasty narrows wide nostrils or a broad nose base by trimming the flare, usually alongside rhinoplasty, and the slimmer base is visible once healed. Forum posters debate how much change a given face needs. Published work is mainly technique reports.

lead: Alar base reduction, usually called alarplasty, is a cosmetic nasal surgery that narrows the width of the nostril flare or the base of the nose by removing small wedges of tissue at the nostril rim or the alar-facial junction. It is performed either on its own or together with rhinoplasty, and surgeons describe it as one of several tools for correcting nostril size and shape.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing culture it is discussed as a hardmaxxing option for people who consider their nostrils too wide or flared. Published literature on the topic consists mainly of surgical technique descriptions and classification studies, including work on how the alar region moves during a smile, rather than controlled trials of cosmetic satisfaction.[3][4]
infobox: Alarplasty, nostril reduction, alar base narrowing

paras: Surgical papers describe alarplasty as excision of a small amount of skin and soft tissue from the nostril sill, the nostril rim or the junction of the nostril wing with the cheek, followed by suturing, to reduce nostril width or flare. A 2001 article on rhinoplasty in patients whose nostrils appear large relative to a small tip proposed analysing the nostril axis and a nostril-to-tip ratio of about 55:45 (with 60:40 considered acceptable), and described the surgical correction as needing more than one component.[1]

A 2026 technique report describes a modified approach in which alar base narrowing and nostril reduction are performed at the same time in Asian rhinoplasty.[5] Surgeons also use alarplasty in functional contexts: one series on external nasal valve collapse used a modified alarplasty combined with columella surgery in severe cases.[6]

A study of a private practice examined how often alarplasty is performed in primary and revision rhinoplasty, indicating that it is a recognised add-on rather than a stand-alone operation in many practices.[7] A 2023 study of 150 Asian women used three-dimensional imaging at rest and during a maximal smile to classify how the alar region changes dynamically, with the aim of informing the choice of alarplasty strategy.[3]

Because the procedure alters the nostril opening, surgeons have examined its effect on breathing. A 2026 cross-sectional study published in Frontiers in Medicine investigated alarplasty and respiratory function.[4] Reports on external nasal valve collapse also note that reducing the nostril opening interacts with airflow, which is why it is discussed alongside functional nasal surgery.[6]

Several PubMed search hits for the term concern veterinary alarplasty in short-nosed dog breeds with airway obstruction; these describe a different species and are not evidence about the cosmetic human procedure.[8]

Human published work includes a classification study of alar dynamics in 150 Asian women,[3] a technique case series for external valve collapse in 37 patients,[6] a practice-based review of how often the procedure is performed,[7] and a 2026 cross-sectional study of respiratory function after alarplasty.[4] No randomised trial comparing cosmetic outcomes with and without alar base reduction was found.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, alarplasty is typically mentioned alongside rhinoplasty in threads where members post before-and-after photographs and ask others to rate the result.[9]
